newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico sees good access to capital markets.
newsitem.headline: Mexico sees good access to capital markets.

text.p: Mexico expects good access to international capital markets next year, which will allow the government to continue with its refinancing plans, said Alejandro Valenzuela, spokesman for the Finance Ministry.

"We expect to have good access to markets that will allow us to continue with our refinancing plans," Valenzuela said at a briefing for reporters a day before the government outlines it economic budget criteria for 1997.
Mexico will continue its proactive policy of refinancing the public debt in order to avoid any problems with a bulge in maturing debt over the next couple of years, Valenzuela said.
The federal government only has $1.4 billion in debt coming due in 1997, but has higher levels of payments in 1998 and 1999.
Valenzuela noted that Mexico's inflation rate could come in at about 26 percent for this year, after reaching 52 percent last year.
The Alliance for Growth, a government, business and labor economic plan for next year, set an objetive of 15 percent for inflation next year and GDP growth of four percent.
Valenzuela said that under present economic conditions, the economy would be able to grow by that much next year.
Although the official government estimate for growth is three percent this year, Valenzuela said many private sector economists are forecasting between 3.5 to 4.0 percent growth.
He noted that there are more people employed now than before the crisis started in 1994.

But he added that if employment is to grow by one million jobs a year to keep pace with the number of people entering the labor force, the economy will have to grow by about five percent, a rate it hasn't reached since the early 1980s.
He said consumer spending is increasing as employment and real salaries grow, and debtor aid programs help spending.
Direct foreign investment is also seen increasing next year, he said.
Budget spending in 1997 is seen at 17 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), with four percent for investment and 13 percent for current spending, one Congressional deputy said at the briefing.
The government sees a public deficit equal to 0.5 percent of GDP in 1997, and a current account deficit of less than 2.0 percent of GDP.
